title: Criterion-Referenced Rubric Builder
problem: Hand-written rubrics drift toward vague, holistic language — 'good analysis', 'clear writing' — that different graders and TAs interpret inconsistently. That inconsistency is the single biggest source of grading-fairness complaints in multi-section courses.

workflow.detail: Write one sentence naming the assignment and the specific outcome it's meant to measure.
Run the Prompt Template to get 3–4 levels per criterion (e.g. Exemplary/Proficient/Developing/Beginning) written in observable, specific language.
Score 2–3 real or sample student submissions against the draft rubric yourself. Note any level where your judgment and the rubric's wording disagree.
Feed each disagreement back as a targeted revision request for that one criterion/level — not a full regeneration of the rubric.
Before rolling out across sections, have a TA or co-instructor score the same sample. If their scores diverge from yours, the rubric language is still too vague.

variables.name: ASSIGNMENT
variables.label: Assignment
variables.placeholder: e.g. 1500-word argumentative essay on a primary source

variables.name: OUTCOME
variables.label: Outcome it measures
variables.placeholder: e.g. Construct a thesis-driven argument supported by textual evidence

variables.name: CRITERIA
variables.label: Criteria to include
variables.placeholder: e.g. Thesis clarity, use of evidence, organization, mechanics

exampleOutput:
| Criterion | Exemplary | Proficient | Developing | Beginning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Thesis clarity | Thesis is arguable, specific, and previewed in the intro | Thesis is arguable but broad or previewed late | Thesis is present but descriptive, not arguable | No identifiable thesis |
| Use of evidence | Every claim cited with a specific passage and explained | Most claims cited; some explanation thin | Evidence present but disconnected from claims | Little to no textual evidence |
tips: If two graders score the same sample differently after using the rubric, the fix is more specific language at the disputed level — not more levels.
For multi-section courses, run the calibration pass with every grading TA before the semester starts, not the week grades are first due.
Reuse the same CRITERIA wording across assignments in a course to build a consistent rubric 'vocabulary' students learn to recognize.
Keep LEVELS to 3–4 — more than that tends to blur into distinctions no grader can reliably apply.
